title: Australia news live: Qantas ground crews vote for right to strike amid pay dispute
text:
NSW police are appealing for information after the body of a newborn baby was found in Sydney’s south-west today.
Officials said emergency services were called to the suburb of Auburn amid reports the baby had been found in a bin. Officers attended and discovered the body of a baby boy.
Police have established a crime scene and commenced an investigation.
They hold serious concerns for the welfare of the baby’s mother and are urging her to attend the nearest hospital to receive urgent care. Police are also asking for anyone with information about the incident, or who was in the area at the time with any relevant footage, to contact police.
Police appeal for mother to come forward after newborn’s body found in Sydney bin
NSW police have called on the mother of an abandoned newborn to come forward after the baby’s body was found in Sydney’s south-west today.
Emergency services were called to the suburb of Auburn after reports that a baby had been found in a bin. Officers attended and discovered the body of a baby boy.
It is believed the child was born within the last 36 hours.
Police have appealed for the unidentified mother to “come forward” or “go immediately to your closest hospital and seek treatment”.
Speaking on 2GB, Auburn police’s Acting Supt Darren Sly said:
Our main focus this afternoon, our priority, is to locate the mother of this child just to ensure that she receives the necessary medical assistance and any other welfare services that she may need.
And of course, we’re also calling for any members of the public who may have been in Harrow Road in the last 36 hours as well … all the small bits of information can be pieced together to hopefully track down this mother.
Qantas ground handling crews may soon walk off the job after overwhelmingly voting in favour of taking industrial action to demand better pay and conditions.
The Transport Workers’ Union (TWU) says 97% of its members employed by Qantas Ground Services (QGS) workers voted for the right to strike in the coming weeks.
QGS is a subsidiary company owned by the airline, set up when Alan Joyce was still its CEO, which – according to the union – pays workers less than its “legacy” workforce.
Its ground crews also perform work for Qantas Freight and the company’s regional Q-Link service, the union says.
The TWU says its health and safety reps in New South Wales have served Qantas with 14 provisional improvement notices over alleged safety failings at Qantas Freight, where a labour hire worker died last year.
The workers voted to strike less than a week after Qantas reported its financial results for the last year, revealing it may hike fares after its profits dipped to a four-year low. The TWU national secretary, Michael Kaine, said:
Last week we saw Qantas crying poor over $2bn in profits, while the board awarded itself a 17% pay rise – but workers and the public see right through it.
These ground workers don’t want to go on strike, but after being sold a false promise that this airline would finally treat them with respect, they’ve got no other choice.
A Qantas spoksperson said:
We remain committed to reaching an agreement with our Qantas Ground Services employees that includes annual pay rises for our people.
We have well developed contingency plans to minimise any impact on customers and our operations, should we be notified of any industrial action.
Discussions through the Fair Work Commission have been constructive and negotiations are continuing.
Liberal shadow minister calls Hanson hypocritical over accusations Labor is inflaming political discourse
The assistant shadow minister for energy, Garth Hamilton, has called One Nation leader Pauline Hanson’s accusation – that the government was “pouring petrol” on inflamed political discourse – hypocritical.
It comes after the One Nation leader accused the prime minister and the treasurer of being “dangerous, divisive and downright dishonest”.
Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Hamilton said:
Senator Hanson has made a career going on Sky News after dark saying much worse things. I’m sure there’s a Labor strategist trawling through the comments she’s made that’s been more strongly worded than ‘dangerous, divisive’ and whatever else it was.
I think there’s a bit of hypocrisy at play. This constant game of I’m the victim. I would remind everybody this is a party that by its own admission is currently infiltrated by extremists.
This is absolutely nonsense, it’s not right. Hypocrisy should be called hypocrisy, and that’s what this is.
That’s all for me! Achol Arok will take things from here.
NSW may not be able to prosecute large-scale water theft
The New South Wales water regulator has cast doubt over its ability to prosecute potential water theft due to uncertainty about the validity of licences governing billions of litres of water entitlements in the state’s north.
It follows a successful legal challenge brought by a group of irrigators in the state’s north-west which found 11 floodplain harvesting licences issued by the former Coalition government were invalid.
The NSW land and environment court found the government had failed to follow correct procedures related to fair consultation with landholders. The case, known as Emu Rider, has raised questions about the validity of the process used to issue hundreds of floodplain harvesting licences.

Kids leaning into AI as literacy levels decline
A majority of Australian youth lack confidence distinguishing news fact from fiction as they increasingly source information from artificial intelligence, AAP reports.
The 2026 News and Young Australians Report, released on Monday, found just 47% of children aged between 10 and 17 felt confident they could spot disinformation online.
A third of the 1,027 kids surveyed had shared a news story on social media to later find it was false.
Data showed youths were less likely to take steps to verify news content than in 2023’s study. Those steps included discussing items, checking multiple stories and changing news sources to more trustworthy outlets.
Declining literacy coincided with increased use of artificial intelligence, the survey also found.
Hanson says Albanese and Chalmers ‘crossed a line’ over criticisms of One Nation
One Nation’s leader, Pauline Hanson, said Anthony Albanese and treasurer Jim Chalmers had “crossed a line” after the prime minister said the party was “peddling politics” that are “dangerous, divisive and downright dishonest” during Queensland’s Labor conference.
Hanson took to social media, writing today:
No matter how worried Jim and Albanese are about losing their jobs, telling Australians that their democratically elected opponents are “dangerous” and a “threat to our country” invites people to treat them as a threat.
Words have consequences. That is how political violence is incited.
The One Nation leader went on to say the pair were “pouring petrol” over inflamed political discourse, warning:
The real danger to Jim and Albanese is that the people of Australia are coming for their government … at the ballot box.
Continuing on from the last post …
The judge criticised the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition of antisemitism as “detached from the reality of the common usage and understanding of antisemitism in this country”.

Australia’s peak Jewish group labelled Fagan’s ruling dangerous judicial “activism” that should be reviewed.

Greens MP Sue Higginson on Monday said:
It was bewildering to see the Minns Labor government signalling they would appeal this decision.
The government’s own legal experts have clearly seen the writing on the wall and told the attorney general that any appeal of this decision would fail.
The New South Wales government will not appeal a supreme court judge’s ruling that rejected the state’s request for a terror order over Mohommed Farhat, who wrote “Fuk Israel” on cars and set another vehicle alight in late 2024.
Last week, Guardian Australia reported that the government was “seeking urgent advice” on the prospects of any appeal after Justice Desmond Fagan had found that disparaging Israel was “political comment”, not antisemitism.
On Monday, the NSW attorney general, Michael Daley, told a budget estimates hearing “we won’t be appealing that decision”.
“Having considered the advice from the crown solicitor, senior and junior counsel, I have reached the conclusion that an appeal would have no reasonable prospects and would fail,” Daley said.
The individual is serving a 20-month sentence in relation to his prior offending and remains in custody.
In his ruling earlier this month, Fagan ruled that police, lower courts and various state agencies all incorrectly labelled Farhat’s actions antisemitic, meaning he was treated more harshly.
From Monday, Queensland has become the first state to make ebike and e-scooter riders hold at least a learner driver’s licence, with new rules kicking in on top of age limits and a statewide police blitz seizing hundreds of non-compliant devices, AAP reports.
Riders must now have a valid learner’s licence to use electric-powered cycles and e-scooters on Queensland roads and paths, with limited exemptions for supervised 12 to 17-year-olds, medically exempt riders and people in designated off-road recreation areas.
“We always said we would make the tough decisions to keep the community safe; our laws get the balance right between cracking down on those who do the wrong thing, while backing those Queenslanders who do the right thing and delivering sensible exemptions,” the state transport minister, Brent Mickelberg, said.
Police have already issued more than 1,700 fines and seized almost 400 illegal devices since 1 July under Operation Yankee Surety, and will now start checking licences during street intercepts.
It is now almost certain the world will warm past 1.5C. But ‘net-negative’ emissions are still possible
Wesley Morgan for the Conversation has written about the greatest threat to the Pacific: climate change.
Anthony Albanese is in Palau this week for the annual Pacific Islands Forum and regional security is expected to top the agenda.
China is testing nuclear-capable missiles in the Pacific, prompting talk of a new regional agreement. The United States-Iran war has exposed a reliance on costly fossil fuels that is undermining Pacific economies.
And as the world comes perilously close to the Paris agreement’s 1.5C temperature goal, a record-breaking El Niño looms in the Pacific Ocean.
Pacific nations will want Albanese to address the world’s key security threat – climate change. As president of negotiations of the Cop31 climate talks in November, Australia can work with the Pacific to keep 1.5C within reach and secure much-needed finance for island nations at the climate frontline.

Michelle Rowland says the government is not immediately planning to ban imports of smartglasses.
The Greens and others have called for the camera-enabled wearable technology to locked out of the country.
The attorney general has told reporters the calls to limit the technology were “valid”. She said:
Firstly, I want to acknowledge the very deep concerns. We are not specifically in this consultation consulting on an import ban. … that would have consequences across government, including across trade, foreign affairs, and other potential legal obligations that can apply internationally.
She said the government’s reforms today would still impact on the smartglasses, with digital platforms prevented from storing recordings and data from the glasses if it was not “fair and reasonable” to do so.
Rowland said she commended local governments who were blocking the glasses’ use, for example at public pools, and said the federal government needed to use the powers that it had.
Let’s be clear, we’re talking about the harmful behaviours and regulating the harms. That’s what governments seek to do. In terms of an import ban, as I said, we are not ruling anything out, but we are utilising what we have at our disposal right now.
The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, is announcing planned new privacy reforms at a Canberra press conference. She has told reporters:
We know that Australians are increasingly concerned about how their data is being collected, used, and shared, particularly as AI and other emerging technologies such as smart glasses become more accessible. People should not have to choose between protecting their privacy and participating in the digital economy.
She said the government was planning to introduce:
A “fair and reasonable” test to limit companies to collecting and using only the personal information they need;
A right to erasure, so people can ask digital platforms to destroy their stores of personal information;
Stronger standards for consent and clearer information when people agree to share personal details;
Limits on businesses buying and selling personal information without clear permission;
And a new ID Lock service through MyGov, designed to let Australians block, unblock, and monitor the use of their eligible identity documents for verification.
Victorian prisoners to be sent out to repair roads under Labor’s pothole plan
Victorian prisoners will be put to work on road maintenance as part of Labor’s plan to fix the state’s potholes if re-elected.
The state’s premier, Ben Carroll, will outline the plan on Monday off the back of an announcement on Sunday that the government would be increasing the road maintenance budget by $352m to fix 500,000 potholes by the end of January.
Carroll will declare that if Labor wins the November election, it would work with Corrections Victoria to develop a pilot program to put supervised, minimum-security prisoners to work performing roadside maintenance.
The plan would include having inmates take over “basic” duties such as mowing lawns, controlling weeds, removing graffiti and picking up rubbish, allowing more skilled crews to focus on fixing potholes.
The government said the work of prisoners “will not replace paid jobs” but instead “supplement the workforce where there are skill and capacity shortages”.
